issues.what: The alt text says each curve rises and then falls, but the df = 2 curve does not rise.
issues.why: For 2 degrees of freedom, the chi-square density is f(x) = (1/2)e^(-x/2) for x ≥ 0. It peaks at x = 0 and decreases monotonically, unlike the df = 4 and df = 10 curves, which rise to interior peaks before falling.

issues.what: The alt text states that 'Each one rises and then falls away...', which is incorrect for the curve with 2 degrees of freedom.
issues.why: A chi-square distribution with 2 degrees of freedom is equivalent to an exponential distribution ($f(x) = 0.5e^{-x/2}$ for $x \ge 0$). It is strictly decreasing from its maximum at $x=0$ and does not rise.

issues.what: The band labelled 95% spans z = −1.5 to 1.5 instead of −2 to 2.
issues.why: For a standard normal distribution, the area within 1.5 standard deviations is approximately 86.6%, not 95%. The shading and area check therefore contradict the 95% label and the alt text stating that this band extends two standard deviations on either side.

issues.what: The second shaded band (representing 95% of the distribution) is drawn from -1.5 to 1.5 standard deviations.
issues.why: According to the empirical rule, approximately 95% of the observations lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean (from -2.0 to 2.0), not 1.5. Drawing the band from -1.5 to 1.5 is mathematically incorrect and misrepresents the standard normal distribution.

issues.what: The alt text and note incorrectly equate density at a value with the probability of that exact value.
issues.why: For a continuous normal random variable, the probability of any exact value is 0. The curve's height is a probability density; probabilities are areas over intervals, not heights at individual points.

issues.what: The alt text and note state that the density (the height of the curve at a single value) is the probability of getting exactly that value.
issues.why: For any continuous random variable, the probability of obtaining any exact single value is 0. The height of the curve represents probability density, not the probability of that specific value. Stating otherwise introduces a major statistical misconception.

issues.what: The figure identifies the shaded right-hand tail as the p-value for a less-than alternative.
issues.why: For Ha: < at z = 1.4, the p-value is P(Z ≤ 1.4) ≈ 0.9192, the area to the left. The shaded right-hand area, P(Z ≥ 1.4) ≈ 0.0808, is the p-value for a greater-than alternative. Thus the subtitle, alt text, and stated p-value contradict the title and the entry's definition.

issues.what: The figure incorrectly associates a 'less-than' alternative hypothesis with the right-hand tail (area above the statistic).
issues.why: For a less-than alternative hypothesis (Ha: <), the p-value is the area to the left of (below) the test statistic, not the area to the right (above) it. The figure shades the region from 1.4 to infinity and labels it as the p-value for 'Ha: less than', which is statistically incorrect and contradicts the authored reference entry.

issues.what: The alt text says the central region is shaded and the tails are unshaded, but the drawing parameters shade the two tails outside ±1.96 instead.
issues.why: The shaded regions contain approximately 5% of the total area, not the 95% confidence region described in the alt text.

issues.what: The alt text contradicts the visual shading of the figure.
issues.why: The 'shade' parameters define shading for the two tails (from -infinity to -1.96, and from 1.96 to infinity), whereas the alt text describes the central region as shaded and the two tails as unshaded.

issues.what: The alt text and note claim that the curves are symmetric and defined for negative values.
issues.why: Chi-square distributions with 2, 4, and 10 degrees of freedom are right-skewed and have no support at negative values. The parameters specify chi-square curves on x = 0 to 22, not symmetric curves extending to both sides of zero.

issues.what: The alt text says each curve rises and then falls.
issues.why: The chi-square density with 2 degrees of freedom has its maximum at zero and decreases monotonically; it does not rise before falling.

issues.what: The note and alt text contain false statistical statements.
issues.why: The note states that the distribution is 'Symmetric about its mean, and defined for negative values as well as positive', and the alt text states that 'Each curve extends to both sides of zero and is symmetric about its centre'. Chi-square distributions are only defined for non-negative values (x >= 0) and are skewed right, not symmetric.
